cards.title: Write a one-paragraph messaging strategy before any copy
cards.summary: A short written messaging strategy gives every copy and design decision a rationale so you stop choosing words by what 'sounds good'.
cards.use_when: You are about to write or rewrite PDP copy, homepage copy or ad creative for a store and need a shared standard for what the copy should do, especially when several people or freelancers touch it.
steps: Before writing any copy, write down the guiding principles your copy must follow as a short document. Joanna Wiebe's example for Page99Test.com is a single paragraph: copy is 'short, friendly and to the point', assumes visitors want to read book excerpts not marketing copy, keeps words to a minimum, and wherever a screenshot, press logo, button, video demo or icon can be used it should replace copy without sacrificing clarity.

Pick the principles that matter for your store from the source's list of candidate principles: let copy guide design because good writing is good design; some visitors want to read a lot and some don't, and both are customers; support messages with social proof like testimonials or media reviews; support key concepts with video demonstrations; just because you say it doesn't make it true, so prove it; strive for clarity above cleverness; let the message match the medium at an exact point of need; all visitors can be persuaded to join or upgrade; engage visitors with content, experiences or mobile/app options.
Treat the document as a living document, not etched in stone: update it as you learn your customers' language and as you add or change products.
Share the strategy with designers, developers and freelancers so they understand your brand and messaging approach before they produce assets.
Draft your own version in one sitting without censoring yourself, then edit afterward rather than trying to reach a final version on the first, second or third try.
caveats: The source frames this for startups; a longer or more detailed strategy is not required for it to work.
The strategy governs copy, not formatting or layout — establish messages before formatting bullets, headlines and buttons.

cards.title: Do customer research before writing a single word of copy
cards.summary: Your store's messages should come from potential customers' language and motivations, not from why you built the product.
cards.use_when: You are preparing PDP copy, ad creative, taglines or a homepage and are tempted to start from internal assumptions about why people buy.
steps: Accept the source's core rule: every message you write needs to be a message your ideal visitors want to see. What you like hearing does not matter; copy that only 'wordsmiths' your internal message can fail to convert no matter how much the team loves it.

Gather customer intelligence instead: if you have an email list from lead gen or pre-launch signups, send a short survey and ask about them and what interests them in the service. The source notes that asking people to do you a 'favor' (and using 'please') can raise response rates, and says to test it.

Alternatively talk to people directly: the source argues that recruiting 8 people at a coffee shop — even with $25 gift cards — is cheaper than a formal focus group and yields real conversations that stick better than a report. Focus groups are also prone to groupthink where a dominant personality skews the data.

Or listen online: participate in forums relevant to your category with the intent to listen to what potential customers discuss and engage only when mutually beneficial — not to spam a launch announcement and leave.
Do not ask customers to approve your copy. The source states that the moment people are aware of copy, everything changes for them, so approval is not a valid test of message.
caveats: The recommendation against asking customers to approve copy refers to reviewing finished copy, not to gathering research from them.
Survey response-rate tips are the source's observed claims, not guaranteed numbers.

cards.title: Define your primary target segment before writing copy
cards.summary: Pick the segment most likely to visit often and to compensate you in cash or referrals, then write for that segment rather than a generic market.
cards.use_when: You are deciding who your homepage, PDP or ad messages should speak to, or you suspect your copy is trying to please everyone.
steps: Challenge your assumed market. The source's example: a photo-sharing startup may assume its market is the early-adopter tech crowd that upvotes the launch post, but research may show the prevailing users are teenage girls, teenage 'EMO' boys, new moms and retired women. Messages that work on tech geeks are unlikely to work on those groups.

Collect demographic and behavioral details for each candidate market: age group, marital status, number of children, education, annual income, average consumer debt load, favorite websites, favorite pastimes, shopping preference (online vs retail vs print catalogue) and tech-savviness.

Segment the market into manageable groups rather than marketing to everyone. The source's chosen segment is the group that will visit with the most frequency and be most likely to compensate you — with money paid or with referrals.

Let the segment shape the message. Example: for married young stay-at-home moms with household income under $55K, high credit-card debt and high tech-savviness, lead with affordability and do not spend message space on ease. For middle-aged career-oriented women with low debt, high income and time on Skirt.com and Oprah.com, do not talk about affordability — the source suggests pricing and messaging might play into high prices equalling better solutions, and ease may be relevant if that segment is not tech-savvy.
Test segment fit with PPC ads targeted at each candidate segment and see which segments click through.
caveats: The income and debt figures in the source's examples are illustrative persona details, not benchmarks.
Costs money to buy segment test traffic; the source treats that as money well spent only if it identifies the best-fit segment.

cards.title: Run a 12-interview pain-point research round
cards.summary: The source cites Stiehl and DeVries' claim that 12–15 one-on-one interviews surface about 80% of a segment's pain points, matching 7 focus groups.
cards.use_when: You need to identify the pains your product copy and ad hooks should address, and are weighing interviews against focus groups.
steps: Recruit 12 to 15 people from your target segment for one-on-one interviews. The source, citing Pain Killer Marketing (2008) by Chris Stiehl and Henry DeVries, says this generates about 80% of all possible pain points for the segment — the same as 7 focus groups of up to 12 participants each.
Run them as conversations rather than questionnaires, so you capture what people reveal about themselves beyond direct answers.

After at least 12 respondents, document and analyze everything. The source warns explicitly not to use this to validate your assumptions — look for new information, and highlight both the surprising and the repeated findings.

Cross-check the pains you hear through other channels: audit competitor sites to see which pains they hit on, use the Google Adwords keyword tool for phrases your audience searches, run PPC ads testing different pain points to see which get clicked most, monitor your segment on Twitter and their blogs, and find out what websites they commonly visit.
Translate each confirmed pain into how your product addresses or eradicates it, and use that in copy.
caveats: The 80% figure is the source's citation of a specific 2008 book, not a measured law; treat 12–15 as a starting heuristic.
Keyword tool names and interfaces may have changed; verify the current tool.
Sources disagree on methods — the source prefers interviews and casual conversations over formal focus groups.

cards.title: Separate pain targeting from motivation reflection in copy
cards.summary: Great copy either neutralizes a critical pain or reflects a deep motivation — motivation is not a discount, a limited-time offer or your value proposition.
cards.use_when: You are drafting headline and hero copy for a PDP or landing page and need to decide whether to hit pain or aspiration.
steps: Recognize the two sides of crafting a message: targeting pain, and reflecting motivation including values. Your product must either address and neutralize or eradicate a critical pain, or pinpoint a key motivation.

Write motivation copy by reflecting, not describing, what drives the visitor. The source's example: Teresa, 39 and 65 pounds overweight, goes to a weight-loss site. Her real motivations are to prove herself against the skinny neighbor, attract an ideal partner, earn her mother's respect and love what she sees in the mirror — but she tells herself she wants information about weight loss. A million sites give information; the smart copy reflects the motivation, e.g. 'Embrace the Woman in the Mirror', supported with photos of two friends smiling coming out of a dressing room, testimonials from real women who love shopping now, and video and print case studies.
Do not write the raw motivation literally (the source rejects 'Become the Size Zero You See in Magazines' as too blunt) — write useful copy that reflects it.

Do not confuse motivation with discount or urgency: the source states that motivation is not a discount or a limited-time offer, and is not your value proposition, because a value proposition speaks to your unique solution while motivation speaks to the customer's pain.

If competitors or a broader category have already created the motivation, piggyback on it rather than recreating it. Example copy given: 'Americans who use software to manage their money sleep better at night', 'Find out where you're leaking cash so you can save more money & invest in your future', 'Categorize your expenses!'
Back any factual claim with a source, such as a link to the article where the research was published.
caveats: Motivation copy may not convert every visitor; the source's stated goals for it are to confirm the solution is what they thought it was, remind them they need a solution, keep them on the page, get them nodding, and move them to the next step.
Pain and motivation lists in the source are illustrative, not exhaustive.

cards.title: Target 20–35% of visitors instead of 100%
cards.summary: Copy written for a narrow, highly qualified segment can convert far better than neutral copy written to offend no one.
cards.use_when: You are writing or revising a homepage headline, PDP headline or ad hook and feel pressure to keep it broad so it does not exclude anyone.
steps: Reject the neutral-house theory for stores. Real estate agents depersonalize a house because they need one buyer for one house; you need hundreds of buyers, which tempts you to neutralize your site into a 'beige blob'. The source's counter-argument: if you try to make every visitor happy you say nothing compelling enough to make anyone buy.
Write for your most qualified traffic — the source's band is 20–35% of visitors, and it states that even 22% is fine to write for.

Do the conversion math as the source frames it: if only 20% of visitors are in the segment and you convert half of them, your conversion rate becomes 10%; converting a quarter of that segment yields 5%, which the source describes as more than double the average for untargeted large-company sites.

Use direct-mail precedent: a piece promoted with 'How to Legally Rob Slot Machines in ANY Casino!' converted well enough to be mailed repeatedly in 2005 by taking the risk of being highly desirable to a select few rather than appealing to everyone.

Revise existing copy to speak directly to that segment. Make headlines more specific at minimum. The source's test: the more neutral and bland your copy is, the more likely you are not targeting a segment.

Take the segment-specific headline pattern from startups the source cites: CampaignMonitor 'Email marketing software for designers and their clients' (any industry could use it, but designers arrive most and are influencers), CollegeBudget 'Student-only deals, delivered daily', Reach.ly 'We connect hotels with guests in real time', Trulia 'Homes and local scoop for the real estate obsessed'.
Once the message is right for the segment, buy more traffic for that segment — the source expects better ROI than sending untargeted traffic to a targeted page.
caveats: The source's conversion arithmetic is illustrative, not a benchmark; the 20–35% band is the source's heuristic.
Do not let narrow targeting lock you out of expansion — the source notes that Reach.ly-style focused messages can be expanded as the business grows.

cards.title: Build a product positioning document with five columns
cards.summary: List every feature, mark which are unique, map each to a customer pain and at least one benefit, then priority-rank the rows.
cards.use_when: You are preparing to write PDP copy, comparison content or in-product messaging and need one source of truth about what your product does and why it matters, or you sell multiple products and need one document per product.
steps: Create a table with five columns: Features, Unique to Us, Customer Pain Solved, Benefits, Priority.

In Features, list every single feature and leave nothing out. Even a feature you consider small — the source's example is a light switch on a lamp — may be the bullet that puts you above a competitor in someone's mind. Do not start writing copy or toying with words at this stage.

In Unique to Us, check the box when only your solution offers the feature; if a competitor offers it, list each competitor; if it is similar to a competitor's feature, briefly describe the similarity.
In Customer Pain Solved, use your earlier customer research to note which pain each feature solves or addresses, and tag which segment it solves for when you have several.

In Benefits, assign at least one express benefit to every feature; some features have several. If a feature has no express benefit and you have to stretch to make one fit, cut it from the list — the customer does not need to learn about it on your site.
Set Priority per row — the source uses high, medium, low or numbers or color-coding — to know what to emphasize versus subordinate when writing.
Create a separate document for each product variant, and reuse the document for every page, email and in-product message.
caveats: The source recommends spending real time making this document thorough and 'possibly ugly' — it is a listing exercise, not a wordsmithing exercise.
Benefits of how you do what you do (e.g. FSC-only paper, a playful bookkeeping look-and-feel, donating to 1% for the Planet, vegan-certified materials) sit outside features and need their own rows.

cards.title: Distinguish features from benefits and write the customer's outcome
cards.summary: A description of what a feature does is not a benefit; the benefit is the value the specific buyer derives from it.
cards.use_when: You are writing PDP bullets or benefit blocks and keep restating specifications instead of outcomes.
steps: Use the source's working definitions: a feature is a part of your product that does a unique thing (a light switch on a lamp); a benefit is the outcome of what that feature does — the value the customer derives (you can easily fill a room with light or darken it).

Avoid the common mistake of treating the purpose of a feature as its benefit. Example: for an online cake service, gluten-free flour that prevents flare-ups for people with celiac and aligns with whole-food or vegan diets is still a description of the feature, not the benefit.

Ask who the buyer is, because the benefit changes per segment. For a grandmother who feels deep satisfaction when loved ones enjoy a meal, the benefit of a gluten-free cake is watching her granddaughter with celiac enjoy her birthday party like every other kid. For a teacher bringing a celebratory cake to school under gluten restrictions, the benefit is rewarding her students while keeping the principal and the PTA happy.
Judge a benefit by whether it tells the customer what is in it for them — how they will feel after using it and what improves in their lives — not merely what the feature will do.
Remember the source's ordering rule for copy: your copy is first about what the user wants, and second about how your product satisfies those wants.
caveats: Benefits that tap into motivations are described as powerful, but the source gives no measured lift figures for benefit-framed versus feature-framed copy.

cards.title: Choose whether to lead with a benefit or a feature per audience
cards.summary: There is no universal rule that copy must lead with the benefit — some shoppers distrust soft benefit language and go straight to comparison charts.
cards.use_when: You are deciding what goes in the hero headline and first bullets of a PDP or landing page for a specific shopper type.
steps: Treat the top-priority message as your 'lead'. The source reports having seen a headline focused on a new product feature outperform a headline showing an expected benefit, so the decision is situational, driven by what your customer base needs at that moment.

Match the lead to shopper type. Some shoppers are suspicious of soft marketing messages — which many benefits unfortunately become. Others jump straight to comparison charts and catalogues to check the features. Others signed up because they heard about one cool feature. The source states none of these types would want you to lead with the benefit.

Whatever you lead with, support every feature with a benefit and every benefit with a feature or a related support point — the source's example of support is a snapshot of the interface design backing a benefit of enjoyable software.

Look at AnyNewBooks as a working pattern: the headline leads with the core benefit, the subhead supports it with the service feature of weekly notifications. The source derives at least three explicit benefits from that one feature: no cost so cash stays in your pocket; weekly cadence means no spam and no wasted seconds deleting emails; the emails come to you so you don't hunt for new books and risk missing something you would love.

Use a mix as Mint does on its How It Works page: the page headline speaks to features while addressing the overarching value proposition of power and simplicity, and the chunk headlines vary between benefits ('See all your accounts in one place', 'stay safe and secure') and features (autocategorization of transactions), each supported by a clear visual.
caveats: The source's cross-reference of feature-led versus benefit-led headline performance comes from the author's own observation, with no dataset, so it does not establish a general rule.

Do not summarize to fit a tight space: the source says a constrained copywriter should choose shorter, tighter words rather than dilute the message, because a summary is neither noticeable nor memorable and specifics stick.

cards.title: Show don't tell: let design and visuals carry part of the message
cards.summary: Some of the strongest messages never appear as text — screenshots and visual design can prove a claim better than copy.
cards.use_when: You are building a PDP, How It Works page or feature section and deciding what to write versus what to show.
steps: Adopt the source's 'show don't tell' reading of Mint: rather than telling visitors the software is design-focused, the site's clean visual design demonstrates the benefit of easy, clean design.

Support each message chunk with a visual that either gives proof of the claim — the source's example is showing interface screenshots — or reinforces the message, as with a sign saying the service is free.
Where a screenshot, press logo, button, video demo or icon can replace copy, let it, but only without sacrificing clarity.

In the product positioning document, pair benefit rows with their support points (e.g. an interface snapshot supporting the benefit of enjoyable software) so writers know what asset to place next to the copy.
Note that good writing is good design in the source's framing — copy should guide design, not be squeezed into a template afterward.
caveats: The source's examples are drawn from Mint and AnyNewBooks as observed at the time of writing; page layouts have since changed.

cards.title: Audit competitor and search language to skip wordsmithing
cards.summary: Messaging built from exact customer keywords, review phrases and competitor audits removes guesswork from value proposition writing.
cards.use_when: You need headline and value-proposition language for a PDP or ad set and are deciding between internal wording and market wording.
steps: Pull language from three external sources rather than from internal assumptions: exact search keywords your audience uses, phrases that appear in reviews, and competitor audits.
Use the Google Adwords keyword tool (verify the current tool name, since interfaces change) to find phrases your audience is searching, as the source recommends for uncovering pain points.
Audit competitors' sites to see which pain points they hit on and which features they claim, and record the overlaps in the Unique to Us column of your product positioning document.

Borrow motivation that competitors or the broader category have already created instead of building it yourself. The source's example: personal finance tools benefit from Intuit, major banks and TV shows like Til Debt Do Us Part having already convinced people they need to manage their money, so the store only has to remind people why they need the solution.
When you make a factual claim in the resulting copy, link or cite the research source — the source suggests this can be as simple as a link to the article where the research was published.
caveats: The source warns against 'wordsmithing' — rearranging internal messages — but does not claim external language alone produces conversion lift.
Competitor copy is itself unverified; treat competitor claims as language input, not as proven positioning.

cards.title: Plan messaging for launch traffic waves
cards.summary: Startup traffic arrives in distinct waves with different motivations, and copy may need lines specifically written to reflect each wave's motivation.
cards.use_when: You are sequencing store launch content, early landing pages or ad campaigns and deciding which message to show as traffic sources shift.
steps: Map the waves the source describes: wave 1 is beta signups from friends, contacts and family who join the email list; wave 2 is media coverage sending specific segments such as developers from Hacker News and technophiles from TechCrunch who also join the list; wave 3 is launch day, when the email list floods the site and many visitors like the site on social networks while niche or foreign press sends a range of traffic; wave 4 brings invitations, blog posts and social recommendations — the 'Lookie Lous'.

Write to the dominant motivation of the current wave. In wave 1, visitors — including a mom who wants to support you and an ex-coworker who wants to pick apart the idea — are looking for the basics of what you are doing. Wave 2 visitors want more specifics. Waves 3 and 4 want to learn about the solution, learn about the company, and identify whether the solution solves X pain for them.
Expect that a value proposition alone may not cover the wave-specific motivation; the source says you will likely have to write lines of copy specifically focused on reflecting visitor motivation.

Write the copy to confirm the solution is what they thought it was, remind them they need a solution like yours, keep them on the page longer, get them nodding, and move them to the next part of the experience where conversion work continues.
caveats: Wave descriptions come from the source's 2011 startup context and media landscape; the sequencing pattern is transferable but the named channels are dated.

cards.title: Test names and creative with cheap ad or shelf experiments
cards.summary: Tim Ferriss' low-budget testing approach — PPC-tested book titles and store-shelf cover tests — transfers to naming products and choosing creative.
cards.use_when: You are choosing a product name, collection name or ad creative set and want market evidence instead of internal preference.
steps: Use paid ad testing to decide naming. The source describes Ferriss buying PPC ads and testing various titles, then using the winning ad's title as the book's name.

Use physical placement to decide creative. Ferriss printed different covers and placed them on other books in a bookstore to see which ones customers gravitated to; the cover that attracted most people became the book's cover.

Translate to ecommerce: test candidate product names or collection names in ad copy and compare click-through; test hero creative variants by exposing them to traffic and watching what people engage with.
Treat these as cheap directional tests rather than definitive design decisions, and rely on the same PPC-through-click testing discipline the source recommends for segment testing.
caveats: The source presents these as examples of low-budget research, not as controlled experiments with reported lift figures.
Ferriss' result — the winning title became the book name — is a case example, not a guarantee that ad-tested names always outperform.

cards.title: Fix headlines that target no one
cards.summary: Copy that could belong to any company in the category signals you are not targeting a segment — make headlines specific.
cards.use_when: You are auditing an existing homepage or PDP headline and it reads generic or interchangeable with competitors.
steps: Check for the failure pattern the source documents: LikeALittle's headline 'Hello! Welcome to LikeALittle! Connect with people near you' describes a campus-only anonymous flirting service but could be confused with any social network's headline. LearnVest's 'Take Control. Afford Your Dreams.' helps women organize their finances yet never mentions women on the homepage — the source calls this a miss.
Contrast with the targeted pattern: CampaignMonitor names designers, CollegeBudget names students, Reach.ly names hotels, Trulia names the real estate obsessed.
Apply the fix: make headlines more specific at minimum. The source's diagnostic is that the more neutral and bland the copy is, the more likely it is not targeting a segment.

Watch for the internal reason for vagueness — being too close to the project, deadline pressure, or believing investors won't fund something too narrow — and treat it as a risk rather than a reason to stay broad.
Recognize the value of being the company that 'gets' a segment: the source argues that if your product is built for one small market segment, own that and speak directly to it.
caveats: The cited sites and headlines reflect their state at the time of writing; some may have changed.
When testing ad copy rather than a durable headline, a broader hook may be appropriate for demand capture — this guidance is about segment-specific messaging, not a ban on any broad ad.

cards.title: Decide whether to write copy in positive or negative framing
cards.summary: Marketing messages typically stem from solving pain, which is inherently negative, while marketing managers push for positive framing — the source flags this tension.
cards.use_when: You are writing PDP or ad copy about a problem the product solves and are choosing between pain-first and positive-outcome-first framing.
steps: Name the tension explicitly: most marketing messages are based on the idea of solving customer pain, which the source calls inherently negative, but marketing managers want messages written in positive ways.

Ask which side of the message you are writing. If you are targeting pain, your job is to neutralize or eradicate a critical pain for the segment. If you are reflecting motivation, the copy should express the desired outcome the visitor is already chasing — the source's example rewrites a blunt desire into 'Embrace the Woman in the Mirror' rather than naming the size-zero aspiration.

Do not substitute discounts or limited-time offers for genuine pain or motivation: the source states motivation is not a discount and not a limited-time offer, even where customers are price-sensitive.

Choose framing based on the segment's shopper type — the same audience that distrusts soft benefit language may respond better to a direct problem statement, while a motivation-led buyer responds better to outcome language.
Keep all claims factual and supported. The source notes that when making claims you must have support, such as a link to where the research was first published.
caveats: The source does not resolve the positive-versus-negative question with a rule; it presents the conflict without prescribing one side.
No measured comparison of positive versus negative copy is provided.

cards.title: Run a research survey and select your target segments
cards.summary: Survey at least 12 people, look for surprising and repeated answers rather than validation, then shortlist segments by visit frequency and compensation.
cards.use_when: You are starting from limited customer knowledge and need to pick which segment your store copy and ads should speak to.
steps: Field a survey by email if you have the list, by phone, or in person at a real location.
Ask questions that get people to reveal themselves — demographics, favorite services and products, and motivations.

Collect at least 12 responses, then document and analyze everything. The source stresses you must not simply validate your assumptions; look for new information that helps you write copy to build the business rather than your ego.
Highlight both the surprising findings and the repeated findings.
Shortlist a segment by two conditions together: they visit your site frequently, and they compensate you with cash or referrals and likes.
Then buy PPC ads on Google targeted to each candidate segment and see which segments click through, accepting that the test costs money but is worthwhile if it pinpoints the single best fit.
caveats: 12 responses is the source's stated minimum for this exercise, not a statistical standard.
Asking respondents to do you a favor and adding 'please' is claimed to raise response rates; the source says to test it.
